entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.7.1-Deut.7.4">Deu 7:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen2229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2230" type="x-p"/> As the Israelites were warned against idolatry in <reference osisRef="Deut.6.14">Deu 6:14</reference>, so here are they exhorted to beware of the false tolerance of sparing the Canaanites and enduring their idolatry. - <reference osisRef="Deut.7.1">Deu 7:1</reference>, Deu 7:5. When the Lord drove out the tribes of Canaan before the Israelites, and gave them up to them and smote them, they were to put them under the ban (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.27.28">Lev 27:28</reference>), to make no treaty with them, and to contract no marriage with them. נשׁל, to draw out, to cast away, e.g., the sandals (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.5">Exo 3:5</reference>); here and <reference osisRef="Deut.7.22">Deu 7:22</reference> it signifies to draw out, or drive out a nation from its country and possessions: it occurs in this sense in the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> in 2Ki 16:6. On the Canaanitish tribes, see at Gen 10:15. and <reference osisRef="Deut.15.20">Deu 15:20</reference>-21. There are seven of them mentioned here, as in <reference osisRef="Josh.3.10">Jos 3:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.24.11">Jos 24:11</reference>; on the other hand, there are only six in <reference osisRef="Deut.20.17">Deu 20:17</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.3.8">Exo 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.17">Exo 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.23">Exo 23:23</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Exod.33.2">Exo 33:2</reference>, the Girgashites being omitted. The prohibition against making a covenant, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.32">Exo 23:32</reference> and <reference osisRef="Exod.34.12">Exo 34:12</reference>, and that against marrying, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.34.16">Exo 34:16</reference>, where the danger of the Israelites being drawn away to idolatry is mentioned as a still further reason for these commands. יסיר כּי, “<hi type="italic">for he</hi> (the Canaanite) <hi type="italic">will cause thy son to turn away from behind me</hi>,” i.e., tempt him away from following me, “<hi type="italic">to serve other gods</hi>.” Moses says “from following <hi type="italic">me</hi>,” because he is speaking in the name of Jehovah. The consequences of idolatry, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.6.15">Deu 6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.26">Deu 4:26</reference>, etc.
entries.content_plain:
Deu 7:1-4 
 
 As the Israelites were warned against idolatry in Deu 6:14, so here are they exhorted to beware of the false tolerance of sparing the Canaanites and enduring their idolatry. - Deu 7:1, Deu 7:5. When the Lord drove out the tribes of Canaan before the Israelites, and gave them up to them and smote them, they were to put them under the ban (see at Lev 27:28), to make no treaty with them, and to contract no marriage with them. נשׁל, to draw out, to cast away, e.g., the sandals (Exo 3:5); here and Deu 7:22 it signifies to draw out, or drive out a nation from its country and possessions: it occurs in this sense in the Piel in 2Ki 16:6. On the Canaanitish tribes, see at Gen 10:15. and Deu 15:20-21. There are seven of them mentioned here, as in Jos 3:10 and Jos 24:11; on the other hand, there are only six in Deu 20:17, as in Exo 3:8, Exo 3:17; Exo 23:23, and Exo 33:2, the Girgashites being omitted. The prohibition against making a covenant, as in Exo 23:32 and Exo 34:12, and that against marrying, as in Exo 34:16, where the danger of the Israelites being drawn away to idolatry is mentioned as a still further reason for these commands. יסיר כּי, “for he (the Canaanite) will cause thy son to turn away from behind me,” i.e., tempt him away from following me, “to serve other gods.” Moses says “from following me,” because he is speaking in the name of Jehovah. The consequences of idolatry, as in Deu 6:15; Deu 4:26, etc.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.7.6-Deut.7.8">Deu 7:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen2231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2232" type="x-p"/> They were bound to do this by virtue of their election as a holy nation, the nation of possession, which Jehovah had singled out from all other nations, and brought out of the bondage of Egypt, not because of its greatness, but from love to them, and for the sake of the oath given to the fathers. This exalted honour Israel was not to cast away by apostasy from the Lord. It was founded upon the word of the Lord in <reference osisRef="Exod.19.5-Exod.19.6">Exo 19:5-6</reference>, which Moses brought to the recollection of the people, and expressly and emphatically developed. “<hi type="italic">Not because of your multitude before all nations</hi> (because ye were more numerous than all other nations) <hi type="italic">hath Jehovah turned to you in love</hi> (חשׁק, to bind oneself with, to hang upon a person, out of love), <hi type="italic">for ye are the littleness of all nations</hi>” (the least numerous). Moses could say this to Israel with reference to its descent from Abraham, whom God chose as the one man out of all the world, whilst nations, states, and kingdoms had already been formed all around (<hi type="italic">Baumgarten</hi>). “<hi type="italic">But because Jehovah loved you, and kept His oath which He had sworn to the fathers, He hath brought you out</hi>,” etc. Instead of saying, He hath chosen you out of love to your fathers, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.37">Deu 4:37</reference>, Moses brings out in this place love to the people of Israel as the divine motive, not for choosing Israel, but for leading it out and delivering it from the slave-house of Egypt, by which God had practically carried out the election of the people, that He might thereby allure the Israelites to a reciprocity of love.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.7.9-Deut.7.10">Deu 7:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen2232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2233" type="x-p"/> By this was Israel to know that Jehovah their God was the true God, the faithful God, who keeps His covenant, showing mercy to those who love Him, even to the thousandth generation, but repaying those who hate Him to the face. This development of the nature of God Moses introduces from <reference osisRef="Exod.20.5-Exod.20.6">Exo 20:5-6</reference>, as a light warning not to forfeit the mercy of God, or draw upon themselves His holy wrath by falling into idolatry. To this end He emphatically carries out still further the thought of retribution, by adding להאבידו, “<hi type="italic">to destroy him</hi>” (the hater), and וגו יאהר לא, “<hi type="italic">He delays not to His hater</hi> (sc., to repay him); <hi type="italic">He will repay him to his face</hi>.” “<hi type="italic">To the face of every one of them</hi>,” i.e., that they may see and feel that they are smitten by God (<hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.7.12-Deut.7.26">Deu 7:12-26</reference> <div eID="gen2234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2235" type="x-p"/> The observance of these commandments would also bring great blessings (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.12-Deut.7.16">Deu 7:12-16</reference>). “<hi type="italic">If ye hearken to these demands of right</hi>” (<hi type="italic">mishpatim</hi>) of the covenant Lord upon His covenant people, and keep them and do them, “<hi type="italic">Jehovah will keep unto thee the covenant and the mercy which He hath sworn to thy fathers</hi>.” In עקב, for אשׁר עקב (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.18">Gen 22:18</reference>), there is involved not only the idea of reciprocity, but everywhere also an allusion to reward or punishment (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.8.20">Deu 8:20</reference>; Num 14:24). חסד was the favour displayed in the promises given to the patriarchs on oath (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.16">Gen 22:16</reference>).
